articles.title: The Ministry of Industry and Trade is seeking feedback on amendments to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg on the structure of retail electricity tariffs. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The Ministry of Industry and Trade is seeking feedback on amendments to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg on the structure of retail electricity tariffs.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Accordingly, following the direction of the Standing Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc in Official Letter No. 9136/VPCP-CN dated September 8, 2026, from the Government Office, the Ministry of Industry and Trade is currently drafting a Decision to amend and supplement several articles of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg dated May 29, 2025, of the Prime Minister regulating the structure of retail electricity tariffs (draft Decision) using a simplified procedure to soon apply the retail electricity tariff structure stipulated in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the peak, off-peak, and normal hours of the national power system as stipulated in Decision 963/QD-BCT dated April 22, 2026.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade is seeking feedback on amendments to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg on the structure of retail electricity tariffs.
The Ministry of Industry and Trade has recently issued Official Letter No. 8615/BCT-DL dated October 19, 2026, to relevant parties requesting their input on the draft Decision amending and supplementing several articles of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg.
The draft Decision amends regulations related to the effective date of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg to promptly apply a new retail electricity pricing structure and peak/off-peak hours to align with the current load profile of the power system.
Article 1 of the draft Decision abolishes the continued application of Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg. According to the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the current retail electricity pricing structure and peak/off-peak hours are still applied according to the regulations in Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg and the Circular guiding Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg. This abolition corresponds to the full implementation and application of the provisions of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg as stipulated in Article 2 of the draft Decision.
The draft Decision also amends and supplements the provisions in Clause 1, Article 7 concerning the effective date of Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg, stipulating that Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg takes effect from a specified date (to be determined when the Prime Minister signs and issues the amending and supplementing Decision), removing the phrase "applicable from the date of the most recent adjustment of the average retail electricity price after the effective date of this Decision" so that the entire content of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg takes effect and is applied in practice from the effective date of the amending and supplementing Decision.
At the time the amended and supplemented Decision takes effect, the entire Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg is replaced by Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the amended and supplemented Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg. Therefore, the retail electricity tariff structure will be applied according to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, and the new peak and off-peak hours will be applied according to Decision 963/QD-BCT from the date the amended and supplemented Decision takes effect.
Clarify the electricity tariff structure for industrial customers with voltages of 220 kV and above.
The draft Decision also replaces the phrase "220 kV voltage level" with the phrase "Voltage level from 220 kV and above" in section 1.1.1 of the Appendix attached to Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg to clarify that the retail electricity tariff structure in section 1.1.1 of the Appendix to Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg applies to manufacturing customers purchasing electricity from a voltage level of 220 kV and above.
Explaining this amendment, the Ministry of Industry and Trade stated that in its submission No. 2318/TTr-BCT dated April 3, 2025, to the Prime Minister regarding the draft Decision on the structure of retail electricity tariffs, the retail electricity prices were explained according to voltage levels as follows: high voltage above 35 kV (including voltage levels above 35 kV to below 220 kV and voltage levels of 220 kV and above), medium voltage from above 1 kV to 35 kV, and low voltage below 1 kV; In fact, in the calculations to determine the retail electricity tariff structure stipulated in Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg (replacing Decision No. 28/2014/QD-TTg), the retail electricity tariff structure for customers purchasing electricity at 220kV voltage level is also the retail electricity tariff structure for customers purchasing electricity at voltage levels above 220kV.
Therefore, according to the calculations in Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg, customers purchasing electricity at 220kV voltage level will have the same price as customers purchasing electricity at voltage levels of 220kV and above. This is also the method used to determine the retail electricity tariff structure in Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg, according to which Section 1.1 of the Appendix attached to Decision 28/2014/QD-TTg stipulates the retail electricity tariff structure applicable to manufacturing customers at "Voltage levels of 110 kV and above".
“Replacing this phrase helps ensure consistency when applying the retail electricity tariff structure to manufacturing customers, avoiding misunderstandings and preventing the exclusion of certain groups. This is not a new policy or regulation, but rather a policy or regulation that was proposed when drafting Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg, consistent with the calculation of the retail electricity tariff structure in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg,” the Ministry of Industry and Trade emphasized.
In addition, the draft Decision also amends and supplements the note on the application period of the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging in the Appendix to Decision No. 14/2025/QD-TTg to conform with the effective date and application of the entire amended Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg.
Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg stipulates that the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging will be applied for a period of 3 years from the date the retail electricity tariff structure under Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg is actually applied as stipulated in Clause 1, Article 7 of Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg. Accordingly, the new structure will only be applied from the date of the first adjustment of the average retail electricity price after Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg comes into effect.
Due to the effective date and application of Decision 14/2025/QD-TT, which has been amended and supplemented as mentioned above, the application period of the retail electricity tariff structure for electric vehicle charging also needs to be adjusted accordingly.
Once the Draft Decision is signed and comes into effect, the retail electricity pricing structure in Decision 14/2025/QD-TTg and the new peak and off-peak hours stipulated in Decision 963/QD-BCT dated April 22, 2025 will be applied immediately.
However, the Ministry of Industry and Trade noted that the immediate application of the new retail electricity pricing structure is not a one-time adjustment of the average retail electricity price. The average retail electricity price remains unchanged at the current rate of VND 2,204.0655/kWh, as stipulated in Decision 599/QD-EVN dated May 7, 2025, of EVN on adjusting the average retail electricity price.

articles.title: How Duty Drawback Can Help Recover the Cost of Forced-Labor Tariffs - Supply Chain Brain
articles.summary: How Duty Drawback Can Help Recover the Cost of Forced-Labor Tariffs  Supply Chain Brain
articles.full_text:
On July 24, 2026, a new set of Section 301 tariffs took effect that few supply chains can sidestep. Following investigations opened on March 12, 2026, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative asserted that dozens of trading partners were failing to impose or enforce bans on goods made with forced labor.
The response was sweeping. The action covers all products from roughly 60 economies, including Canada, Mexico, the European Union, United Kingdom, China, India, Japan and Switzerland, at an added rate of either 10% or 12.5% depending on the country of origin.
For importers, the immediate concern is cost. These are additional duties, and for most goods they’re layered on top of the rates that importers already owe. There are exemptions, and USTR added hundreds of products to that list before the effective date, covering items such as certain seeds, fertilizer and pesticide inputs, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, pharmaceuticals and used clothing. Even so, the majority of goods from the listed economies now carry the extra charge.
It's worth being precise about what these tariffs are. They’re trade-remedy duties assessed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. They’re not the same as the forced-labor import prohibitions enforced under Section 307 of the Tariff Act or the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, which stop non-compliant goods at the border entirely. The Section 301 tariffs apply to goods that are admissible and lawfully entered. That distinction matters, because duties paid on lawfully entered goods can often be recovered later. Goods barred from entry cannot.
The recovery mechanism is duty drawback, which refunds up to 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on imported merchandise when that merchandise, or a qualifying substitute, is later exported or destroyed. It’s one of the oldest programs in U.S. trade law, created so that goods passing through the U.S. on their way to a foreign market aren’t permanently burdened by U.S. import duties.
Section 301 duties are eligible for drawback. This sets them apart from Section 232 steel and aluminum duties and Section 201 safeguard duties, which are not recoverable through drawback, and from antidumping and countervailing duties, which are also excluded. Because the new forced-labor tariffs are Section 301 duties, importers who export can pursue a refund on the portion of their goods that leaves the country.
The most direct route is unused merchandise drawback. If a company imports a product, pays the Section 301 duty, and then exports or destroys that product without using it in the U.S., it can claim back up to 99% of the duty. The goods don’t have to be the exact ones imported. Substitution rules let a company match imports and exports that share the same eight- or 10-digit Harmonized Tariff System classification, which adds flexibility for busy operations.
The second route is manufacturing drawback. Here, a company imports components or raw materials, uses them to produce a finished article, and exports that article. The duties paid on the imported inputs, including the Section 301 charge, become recoverable once the finished product is exported. This is common in industries that bring in parts and ship out assembled goods.
Both paths reach back further than many importers expect. A drawback claim can generally cover imports from the previous five years, so duties already paid on past entries aren’t necessarily lost.
Many companies affected by the forced-labor tariffs aren’t simply selling into the U.S. market. They re-export, supply foreign customers, and run global manufacturing that moves goods back out of the country. For those flows, drawback turns a portion of the new tariff from a sunk cost into a refund. It doesn’t erase the tariff, and doesn’t apply to goods consumed domestically, but on the exported share it can return nearly the full amount.
A few practical points. Documentation is everything. Customs and Border Protection reviews drawback claims tied to Section 301 duties closely, and clean records that link specific imports to specific exports are what carry a claim. Antidumping and countervailing duties on the same goods remain off the table. And, because eligibility turns on specifics such as classification, export evidence and timing, a review of your own import and export history is the only reliable way to assess the opportunity.
The forced-labor tariffs are broad, and will remain in force while the legal challenges filed against them work through the courts. Classification review and exemption checks belong in any response. So does drawback, which for exporters is often the single largest lever available to recover what these new duties add at the border.
Tony Nogueras is founder and chief information officer of Alliance Drawback Services.

October 16, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (the “Act”),[1]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,[2]
notice is hereby given that on October 13, 2026, Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Exchange filed the proposal as a “non-controversial” proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act [3]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6) thereunder.[4]
The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
Cboe EDGX Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe EDGX” or the “Exchange”) is filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission” or “SEC”) a proposed rule change to amend Rule 11.1(a)(3) to describe when unpriced orders are eligible for execution and to amend Rule 11.6(q)(2) to clarify the expiration of Day Orders entered during the Overnight Trading Session or Order Acceptance Queueing Time. The text of the proposed rule change is provided in Exhibit 5.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 11.1(a)(3) to introduce rule text to describe when orders that do not contain a limit price are eligible for execution. Under current Rule 11.1(a)(1), the Exchange does not accept Market Orders,[5]
other than those with a Time-in-Force (“TIF”) instruction of Regular Hours Only [6]
or a Stop Price, prior to 4:00 a.m. Eastern Time or prior to 7:00 a.m. Eastern Time for orders eligible for a 7:00 a.m. Start.[7]
As part of the Exchange's transition to trading 23 hours per day, 5 days per week (“23x5 Trading”), the Exchange updated Rule 11.1(a) to introduce a new subparagraph (3) titled “Orders Permitted in Each Session.” [8]
Rule 11.1(a)(3), which is approved but not yet effective, states: “Market Orders, other than those designated with a Time-in-Force instruction of Regular Hours Only or those that include a Stop Price, will not be accepted by the Exchange prior to Regular Trading Hours.” The intent of this sentence was to prevent Market Orders from executing during the Overnight Trading Session [9]
and the Pre-Opening Session,[10]
but the text did not expressly prohibit the Exchange from accepting Market Orders during Regular Trading Hours and executing during the Post-Closing Session,[11]
which experiences similar characteristics regarding liquidity and volume as the current Early Trading Session.[12]
Now, the Exchange proposes to add an additional sentence to the end of Rule 11.1(a)(3) which states: “Orders without a limit price will not be eligible for execution outside of Regular Trading Hours.” The addition of this sentence eliminates any potential ambiguity about when an order that does not contain a limit price will be eligible for execution on the Exchange. In addition, this proposed change is substantially similar to limits on unpriced orders currently in place on Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (“Nasdaq”) and NYSE Arca, Inc. (“NYSE Arca”) and differs only in that the Exchange's proposed rule refers to orders without a limit price rather than specifically designating market orders or pegged orders as other market centers have done in their rule text.[13]
The Exchange also proposes to amend Rule 11.6(q)(2) to clarify that a Day Order entered during the Order Acceptance Queueing Time [14]
or Overnight Trading Session will expire at the end of Regular Trading Hours on the same business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs, as provided in Rule 11.1(b).[15]
This amendment replaces the phrase “following trading day,” which could be read ambiguously for orders entered after midnight during the Overnight Trading Session, with language that expressly ties the order's expiration to the business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs.
The change is consistent with the Exchange's intent as described in the Original Filing, which introduced the 23x5 Trading framework and explained that “a trading day is deemed to begin at 9:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the preceding calendar day.” Under Rule 11.1(b), a business day includes the Overnight Trading Session on the preceding calendar day, meaning the entire Overnight Trading Session (from 9:00 p.m. through 4:00 a.m.) belongs to the following business day. The proposed amendment merely conforms the Day Order TIF definition to this structural principle and does not alter any operational aspect of Day Order handling.
Specifically, current Rule 11.6(q)(2) provides that a Day Order entered during the Order Acceptance Queueing Time or the Overnight Trading Session “will expire at the end of Regular Trading Hours on the following trading day.” The Exchange proposes to replace “following trading day” with “same business day to which the Overnight Trading Session belongs, as provided in Rule 11.1(b).” This revision eliminates any potential ambiguity regarding whether an order entered after midnight
i.e.,
during the portion of the Overnight Trading Session occurring on a new calendar day) could be interpreted as expiring on a different business day than intended.

What to know about the Iran war today:
The U.S. military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Iran-backed Houthis and direct threats from Iran, sources tell CBS News Wednesday.The latest attack targeted King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam, killing at least one person and injuring eight others Wednesday evening, Saudi officials said.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue over a seven-day ceasefire proposal that President Trump initially rejected last month, with the U.S. seeking new clauses.A senior official with Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened Wednesday to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz and other U.S. "investments" if the U.S. launches new strikes on Iranian infrastructure.Despite global oil prices remaining near five-month highs, President Trump insisted Tuesday that "we're doing very well" with Iran, adding that he was yet to "make a final decision of which way do we want to win" the war, "the nice way or the not nice way."
One killed, 8 injured in Dammam airport attack, Saudis say
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
U.S. troops reducing footprint at Middle East posts, sources say
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
The U.S. State Department has also ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia, citing threats posed by the Iran-backed Houthis.
CBS News has learned several U.S. embassies in the Middle East have adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status.
The restricted operations status, which the department introduced in August amid flare-ups in the war with Iran, allows embassies to reduce staffing and services without fully suspending operations.
Debris from intercepted drone kills 2 in Saudi Arabia, energy ministry says
The Saudi energy ministry said that falling debris from the interception of a drone targeting an oil facility killed two people and injured two others on Wednesday.
"The attempted attack resulted in the deaths of two individuals, a Filipino and a Nepali, and injuries to two others," the ministry said in a statement. It did not say who launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the UAE border.
State Department orders some U.S. government employees and family members to leave Saudi Arabia
The U.S. has ordered all non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces escalating attacks by Houthi militants.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post Wednesday.
The order came a few days after the U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting.
"The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them," Pigott added.
U.S. will suffer "even greater strategic failure" if it chooses war over diplomacy, Iranian FM says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X, sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
U.S. sanctions Greek law firm for alleged involvement in Iranian "shadow fleet"
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast.
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
Riyadh airport partially reopens after deadly Houthi strike
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iran criticizes potential Egyptian involvement in Yemen war; Sisi promises only defensive actions
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's new defense minister says first priority is meeting air force needs
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
Trump blocked Netanyahu's plan for multiday strikes on Iran, report says
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times.
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.

articles.title: Thai industry and MICE agencies join forces to expand global trade and investment - Pattaya Mail
articles.summary: Thai industry and MICE agencies join forces to expand global trade and investment  Pattaya Mail
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK, Thailand – The Federation of Thai Industries (FTI) and the Thailand Convention and Exhibition Bureau (TCEB) have signed an agreement to expand international trade and investment through meetings, conventions, and exhibitions. The partnership will connect Thai manufacturers, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, with overseas buyers, investors, and advanced technologies.
FTI Chairwoman Pimjai Leeissaranukul and TCEB President Dr. Supawan Teerarat signed the agreement on October 20. Pimjai presented plans to use FTI’s network of more than 16,000 businesses across 48 industrial groups and 76 provincial industrial councils to expand market access and generate new commercial opportunities.
Dr. Supawan also detailed TCEB’s role in attracting international business events and connecting Thai enterprises with global partners. The cooperation will cover trade exhibitions, business matching, access to financing and technology, and sharing industry information. Regional exhibitions are also planned for 2027, supported by Thailand’s 16 designated MICE cities.
Thailand welcomed 27.18 million business event travelers during fiscal year 2026, generating approximately 150.9 billion baht in revenue. Both organizations expect the partnership to create more export and investment opportunities while supporting regional businesses and environmentally responsible events. (NNT)

articles.title: SCCI showcases Sharjah's investment potential in food manufacturing industry at SIAL Paris 2026 - Big News Network.com
articles.summary: SCCI showcases Sharjah's investment potential in food manufacturing industry at SIAL Paris 2026  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
SHARJAH, 21st October, 2026 (WAM) -- The Sharjah Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCI), represented by the Sharjah Exports Development Centre, took part in SIAL Paris 2026, one of the world's leading international food trade shows, held in Paris, France, from 17 to 21 October.
The participation reflects SCCI's commitment to expanding the reach of national products in global markets, creating new export opportunities for food and beverage companies, and fostering partnerships with international businesses and manufacturers.
SCCI represented the Emirate of Sharjah at SIAL Paris 2026 with a pavilion featuring government and private sector entities and leading national food manufacturing and trading companies based in Sharjah. Participants included Sharjah Agricultural and Livestock Production Establishment (EKTIFA), Hamriyah Free Zone Authority, Sharjah Airport International Free Zone Authority (SAIF Zone), and the companies "Al Mehwar" and PSL.
The delegation was led by Mohammad Ahmed Amin Al Awadi, Director-General of SCCI, and comprised Ali Abdullah Al Jari, Director of the Sharjah Exports Development Centre, and Maha Mansour Al Zarouni, Senior Exhibitions Executive.
The Sharjah Chamber showcased promising investment opportunities in Sharjah's food manufacturing sector, highlighting the diversity of locally produced products and their potential to scale up and penetrate new international markets. The emirate's industrial base comprises more than 3,000 factories, with advanced food manufacturing facilities representing over 25% of the total, supplying products to a wide range of global markets.
As part of its participation, the Sharjah Chamber conducted a series of business meetings with international companies, manufacturers and investors attending the exhibition. Discussions focused on exploring opportunities for cooperation and commercial partnerships and exchanging expertise on the latest trends and innovations shaping the food manufacturing sector. The Chamber also presented its services and programmes supporting the business community, highlighting the facilities and incentives available to investors.
Mohammad Ahmed Amin Al Awadi said the Sharjah Chamber's participation in SIAL Paris 2026 supports its strategic objectives of strengthening the competitiveness of Sharjah's economic sectors and unlocking new growth opportunities by building strategic partnerships with international markets.
He noted that the food manufacturing sector is a key industry offering significant potential for development and innovation, particularly amid increasing global demand for food products and the heightened focus on diversifying supply chains and enhancing their efficiency.
SIAL Paris 2026 is one of the leading international exhibitions dedicated to the food and beverage industry, bringing together companies, manufacturers, distributors, investors and experts from across the world.

articles.title: U.S. Solar Tariffs Lift Hanwha, OCI Outlook - Businesskorea
articles.summary: U.S. Solar Tariffs Lift Hanwha, OCI Outlook  Businesskorea
articles.full_text:
U.S. Duties on Imports from India, Indonesia, and Laos Reach 268% While Non-Chinese Supply Chains Gain Attention as Washington Tightens Solar Rules
As the U.S. has decided to impose high tariffs of up to 268% on solar products from India, Indonesia, and Laos, the non-Chinese supply chain competitiveness of Hanwha Solutions and OCI Holdings is drawing attention. Analysis indicates that the importance of local U.S. production facilities and the ability to procure non-Chinese raw materials is growing, coupled with the implementation of the U.S. minimum import price system for solar products and China’s push for export controls on core manufacturing technologies.
According to foreign media and the industry on Oct. 21, the United States International Trade Commission (USITC) recently ruled that the U.S. industry suffered damages due to imports of solar cells and modules from India, Indonesia, and Laos. Previously, the anti-dumping and countervailing duty rates calculated by the U.S. Department of Commerce reached 147.06% to 268.06% by company.
The U.S. is also scheduled to implement the minimum import price (MIP) system for solar products under the Trade Expansion Act starting this December. The standards are $21 per kilogram for polysilicon, $0.22 per watt (W) for cells, and $0.38 per W for modules. An additional tariff of 15% will also be applied to some solar-related imports. This is a measure to induce domestic production within the U.S.
China has also released an amendment to add 12 solar technology items, including perovskite-silicon tandem cells and polysilicon manufacturing technologies, to its export ban and restriction list. Although it is currently in the opinion-gathering stage, if the regulations are confirmed, it could affect the establishment of manufacturing facilities and the securing of technology by overseas companies that rely on Chinese technology.
In accordance with such regulatory changes, the possibility is raised that the business conditions of domestic solar companies that have secured U.S. production facilities and non-Chinese raw material supply chains will improve.
Hanwha Solutions is establishing a local supply chain centered on its solar production facilities in Georgia, U.S. Its module production capacity in the U.S. is estimated at 8.6GW annually, while ingots, wafers, and cells are estimated at 3.3GW each. Analysis suggests that if the price negotiation power of U.S.-made products increases, it could help improve the profitability of local production facilities.
However, assessments suggest that whether the manufacturing sector’s performance will improve remains to be seen. Samsung Securities forecasted Hanwha Solutions’ operating profit for the third quarter of this year at 228 billion won (about $172.05 million), while expecting an operating loss of 127.3 billion won in the solar module manufacturing sector. It is pointed out that the key will be how much the tax credit benefits resulting from the rise in the operation rate and the increase in production volume of U.S. production facilities will reduce the cost burden of the manufacturing sector.
Hanwha Qcells has equipped its Jincheon plant in North Chungcheong Province, South Korea, with an annual production capacity of 5.3GW for cells and 2.8GW for modules. It aims to begin mass production of next-generation perovskite-silicon tandem cells and modules at the end of 2028.
OCI Holdings is expanding its non-Chinese supply chain through polysilicon production facilities in Malaysia and wafer production facilities in Vietnam. A representative example is its confirmation in July of an expansion plan to increase the polysilicon production capacity of its Malaysian subsidiary, OCI Terrasus, from the existing 35,000 tons to 70,000 tons per year.
OCI Holdings has also signed a long-term supply contract with a U.S. big tech company. Analysis indicates that as U.S. import regulations are strengthened, the demand for supply chains with low reliance on Chinese raw materials could increase.
An industry official forecasted, “The impact of U.S. protectionist trade measures on corporate performance will vary depending on future production volume and sales prices,” adding, “If the prices of imported solar products rise, the price competitiveness of local manufacturers could improve, but the facility investment costs of power generation business operators and some raw material procurement costs could also increase together.”

articles.title: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s tariffs on Canada - EverythingGP
articles.summary: New lawsuit filed challenging Trump’s tariffs on Canada  EverythingGP
articles.full_text:
A U.S. food importer has filed a lawsuit in the United States Court of International Trade challenging U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs targeting Canada.
The lawsuit, filed Tuesday by the non-profit Liberty Justice Center on behalf of Gellert Global Group in the New York-based court, argued Trump’s use of a Depression-era trade statute exceeds his power as president.
“No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required,” Liberty Justice Center CEO Sara Albrecht said in a news release.
Trump used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap an array of Canadian goods with a 50 per cent levy after trade talks broke down in August.

articles.full_text:
The global supply chain for critical minerals is undergoing a significant shift as the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) recalibrates its role in the cobalt market. Historically, control over essential resources has served as a primary lever of geopolitical influence, a dynamic that remains central to modern industrial and technological security.
The recent implementation of export caps by the DRC, following a period of extreme market volatility and price fluctuations, highlights the tension between resource-rich nations and the processing hubs that dominate the supply chain.
With China currently refining approximately 80% of the world’s cobalt, the Congolese government's decision to restrict supply represents a strategic move to address long-standing economic imbalances and exert greater control over national assets.
This development has prompted rapid maneuvering from international powers. The United States has engaged in new diplomatic and commercial agreements with the DRC, aiming to diversify supply chains and establish domestic refining capacity—most notably with planned infrastructure in Arizona.
This initiative reflects a broader international effort to mitigate dependencies on existing refining monopolies, particularly as cobalt remains indispensable for electronics, defense technology, and green energy sectors. As demand continues to outpace current supply, the competition for secure, reliable access to these resources continues to redefine strategic partnerships and industrial policy across the globe.

articles.title: 12th Southern Industry and Trade Conference: Unlocking Resources, Creating Momentum for Double-Digit Growth - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: 12th Southern Industry and Trade Conference: Unlocking Resources, Creating Momentum for Double-Digit Growth  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
On the morning of October 22, 2026, in Ho Chi Minh City, the Ministry of Industry and Trade organized the 12th Conference of Industry and Trade Sectors of Southern Provinces and Cities - 2026, focusing on evaluating the results of tasks performed in 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, while also identifying key tasks and solutions for the last three months of 2026.
Attending the conference, on behalf of the Ministry of Industry and Trade were Deputy Minister Phan Thi Thang; and representatives from various departments, bureaus, and units under the Ministry of Industry and Trade. On behalf of Ho Chi Minh City were Deputy Secretary of the City Party Committee Nguyen Sinh Nhat Tan; Member of the Standing Committee of the City Party Committee and Permanent Vice Chairman of the City People's Committee Nguyen Loc Ha; and representatives from the Economic and Budget Committee of the City People's Council, the City People's Committee Office, and various departments and agencies. Also present were representatives from the Departments of Industry and Trade of provinces and cities in the Southern region; and leaders of industry associations and businesses.
The conference is themed “Strengthening regional cooperation to unlock resources and contribute to double-digit economic growth in the period 2026 - 2030”.
In 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, despite facing numerous fluctuations in the global economy, adjustments in tariff policies of some major economies, rising input costs, and pressure for green and digital transformation , the Industry and Trade sectors of provinces and cities in the region proactively and flexibly implemented a comprehensive set of solutions to overcome difficulties for businesses, promote production, and expand markets.
Industrial production, trade, and exports maintained their growth momentum.
In 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, the Industry and Trade sectors of provinces and cities in the Southern region will implement solutions to remove difficulties for businesses, promote production, and expand markets. Localities will leverage their strengths in processing and manufacturing industries, high technology, logistics, agricultural and aquatic product exports, renewable energy, and border trade; while simultaneously strengthening supply and demand connections, organizing focused promotional programs, and enhancing the application of information technology and digital transformation in state management.
According to the report on the performance results for 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, and the tasks and solutions for the fourth quarter of 2026 of the Industry and Trade sector in the southern provinces and cities, the industrial production index (IIP) of the region is projected to increase by 11.1% in 2025 compared to the same period. Of these, five out of eight provinces and cities will have higher growth rates than the national average, with the national average being 9.2%. Specifically, Can Tho City will increase by 10.4%; An Giang province by 12.9%; Dong Thap province by 13.1%; Tay Ninh province by 14.9%; and Dong Nai City by 15.2%.
Several industrial products maintained relatively high production levels compared to the same period last year, contributing to the overall growth of the sector. Processed seafood production in Ca Mau increased by 11.8%, Dong Thap by 11.6%, and An Giang by 18.1%. Milled rice production in Can Tho City increased by 3.5%, Tay Ninh by 15.3%, Dong Thap by 8.5%, and An Giang by 8.8%. Footwear production in Can Tho City increased by 10.9%, Dong Nai City by 15%, and Dong Thap by 14.4%.
In the first nine months of 2026, industrial production in the region continued to maintain growth compared to the same period in 2025. The industrial production index for the entire region increased by 12.9%; 6 out of 8 provinces and cities achieved a growth rate higher than the national average of 12.3%. Specifically, Dong Nai City increased by 12.6%; Ca Mau by 12.7%; Dong Thap by 13%; An Giang by 13.7%; Vinh Long by 14.4%; and Tay Ninh by 15%.
In the trade sector, the region's total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue in 2025 is projected to reach VND 3,927,598 billion, an increase of 16.5% year-on-year, accounting for 56.03% of the total retail sales of goods and consumer service revenue nationwide. In the first nine months of 2026, this figure is projected to reach VND 2,858,823 billion, an increase of 16.5% year-on-year, accounting for 48.2% of the national total.
Goods exports continue to maintain their growth momentum. In 2025, the total export value of the Southern region is expected to reach US$167.4 billion, an increase of 7.6% year-on-year, accounting for 35.2% of the country's total export value. In the first nine months of 2026, the export value is estimated to reach US$138.4 billion, an increase of 10.9% year-on-year. Of this, Ho Chi Minh City will account for US$76 billion, Dong Nai City for US$27.5 billion, and Tay Ninh for US$15.5 billion.

The report also stated that businesses continue to leverage tariff preferences from free trade agreements to increase price competitiveness and expand market share in various markets. Monitoring and updating trade policies, trade defense measures, technical standards, environmental standards, traceability requirements, and new regulations of import markets are identified as areas requiring continued attention.
Strengthening regional linkages and developing industrial and energy infrastructure.
Developing industrial, commercial, and energy infrastructure is one of the topics mentioned in the report on the performance of the Industry and Trade sector in the Southern region. Localities continue to implement solutions to develop industrial parks, economic zones, industrial clusters, commercial infrastructure, and electricity supply systems to serve production and business.
Regarding industrial clusters, the region has 93 operational industrial clusters with a total area of 4,216 hectares; and 166 established industrial clusters with a total area of 8,574.9 hectares. In the first nine months of 2026, Tay Ninh established 9 new industrial clusters; Dong Thap implemented the Thanh Tan industrial cluster with an area of 50 hectares and a total investment of over 871.6 billion VND; and Vinh Long implemented 6 new industrial clusters.
Commercial infrastructure continues to be maintained and developed. The entire region has 2,305 markets, 429 supermarkets, 108 shopping centers, and 5,648 convenience stores. This system serves the circulation and distribution of goods and meets consumer needs in the localities within the region.
In the energy sector, commercial electricity output in 2025 is projected to reach 103,051.1 million kWh. In the first nine months of 2026, commercial electricity output is expected to reach 94,687.6 million kWh. Local authorities continue to prioritize the implementation of power grid projects; in Vinh Long, land clearance has been completed for 4 out of 7 110 kV power line projects.
Regarding support for businesses and rural industrial establishments through industrial promotion and industrial development consulting activities, in 2025, the provinces and cities in the Southern region will implement a total budget of VND 38.519 billion, reaching 51% of the annual plan. Of this, the national industrial promotion budget is VND 9.624 billion, and the local industrial promotion budget is VND 28.895 billion.
The total approved budget for industrial promotion in 2026 for provinces and cities in the Southern region is 71.056 billion VND. Of this, the planned local industrial promotion budget is 54.898 billion VND, accounting for 77.3%; and the national industrial promotion budget is 16.158 billion VND, accounting for 22.7%.
In the first nine months of 2026, the budget for industrial promotion reached VND 34.141 billion, equivalent to 48% of the annual plan and 4.61 times higher than the same period in 2025. Industrial promotion, trade promotion, supporting industries, and business support activities continued to be implemented within the state management work of the Ministry of Industry and Trade at the local level.
Focus on overcoming difficulties and completing tasks in the last three months of 2026.
In the last three months of 2026, the Industry and Trade sectors of provinces and cities in the Southern region will focus on achieving growth targets, closely adhering to the double-digit GRDP growth scenario of each locality; regularly updating the production and business situation, clearly identifying industries, enterprises, and projects with the potential to generate growth in order to focus support and address difficulties.
According to the report's tasks and solutions for the fourth quarter of 2026, the Departments of Industry and Trade need to strengthen coordination, inspection, supervision, and evaluation of implementation progress; promptly report to the People's Committees of provinces and cities on issues beyond their authority; focus resources on completing the 2026 targets, creating a foundation for implementing the tasks of developing the industry and trade sector in 2027.

articles.summary: Middle East oil exports climb back to prewar levels  Financial TimesMore Oil is Flowing Through the Persian Gulf Than Before the War. Prices are Still High.  Yahoo FinanceMiddle East Oil Flows Near Prewar Levels Defy Hormuz Attacks  Bloomberg.comHigher Oil Availability Pressures Middle East Crude Benchmarks  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comOil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf like before the Iran war. Why prices may still not come down anytime s...
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the Oil & Gas industry myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Middle Eastern oil exports have returned to prewar levels as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz targeted in the conflict.
In the week to October 18, shipments from Gulf oil producers excluding Iran averaged 24.6mn barrels a day, higher than the 23.3mn prewar average, according to data compiled by Kpler.
That takes the seven-day average for exports to its highest level since mid-February, days before the US and Israel struck Iran, igniting a war that has stymied exports from the world’s biggest oil-producing region.
The figures, which are preliminary, are far more volatile than before the war. They include the Strait of Hormuz — through which the vast majority of the region’s prewar exports passed — as well as ship-to-ship transfers just beyond the narrow waterway and flows from Red Sea ports.
Shipments through Hormuz itself are still more than a third lower than before the war, the data shows.
Despite the rebound in the region’s exports, the oil price has been rising in recent months as markets for some oil products show increasing signs of strain, and on Tuesday Brent crude, the international benchmark, hit its highest level since May. On Wednesday it traded at $108.77 a barrel, flat on the day.
Saudi Arabia routed a lot of oil through its Red Sea port of Yanbu in response to attacks on ships sailing through the Gulf, but flows through this alternative route have dipped periodically in response to attacks on the pipeline that serves the port and on nearby ships. For instance, flows through Yanbu were lower following an attack in mid-September on the pipeline that connects Saudi oil production to the port. Those volumes have since rebounded after Saudi Aramco completed repair work on the pipeline.
Oil exports from the region have remained buoyant this month despite an uptick in attacks on vessels. UK Maritime Trade Operations, which monitors such incidents, has reported 28 attacks on shipping in the region in October, after 18 were recorded over September.
Two ships were targeted on Tuesday night, according to maritime security sources. One tanker was hit in the north of the Gulf near the Iraqi coast, showing the expansion of Iran’s attack range. The vessel was in the vicinity of Khor Al Zubair port, according to maritime security company Vanguard.
The second was struck in the early hours of the morning off the Omani coast, according to an alert from the Pakistani Navy.
Both of the crews were reported safe, despite a fire on board one, which was subsequently put out, maritime security company Vanguard said.

China’s Q3 2026 GDP accelerated from the second quarter thanks to strong exports and high-tech manufacturing. This analysis examines industrial growth, consumer demand, trade trends, and the implications for companies operating in China.
China’s economy in the second quarter.
Across the first three quarters, GDP expanded 4.6 percent year-on-year, putting growth firmly within the annual target between 4.5 and 5 percent set by the government in March.
Speak to an Expert
Identify opportunities and market entry pathways to China’s fast-growing high-tech sectors.
The acceleration has been largely attributed to a boom in tech-related industrial sectors and exports, both of which grew rapidly in September. Domestic consumption, meanwhile, has remained sluggish, although services sales show positive signs.
In the short term, the surge in industrial output and exports signals growing opportunities in technology and advanced manufacturing, although systemic risks remain from cost pressures, changes to global demand, and supply chain disruptions.
Longer term, China’s GDP growth is expected to continue its managed slowdown as the economy matures and high-growth, labour-intensive manufacturing gives way to services and higher-value sectors. For businesses, this shift means recalibrating the role of China-based production within regional and global supply chains, and investing more in higher-value capabilities such as automation, advanced manufacturing, and services.
China’s Q3 2026 Economy at a Glance
GDP growth:
- Q3: RMB 37.54 trillion (US$5.62 trillion); +4.5% yoy
- Q1–Q3: RMB 107.1 trillion (US$16 trillion); +4.6% yoy
Industry:
- Q1–Q3 industrial added value: +5.3% yoy
- Q1–Q3 manufacturing added value: +5.7% yoy; of which:
  - Equipment manufacturing: +10.2% yoy
  - High-tech manufacturing: 14.3% yoy
Consumption:
- Q1–Q3: Retail sales (goods): RMB 37 trillion (US$5.54 trillion); +1.1% yoy
- Q1–Q3: Retail sales (services): +5% yoy
Foreign trade (September):
- Q1–Q3: US$5.8 trillion; +23.8 yoy
- September: US$760.94 billion; +34.1% yoy; of which:
  - Q3 exports: US$447.18 billion; +36.3% yoy
  - Q3 imports: US$313.65 billion; +31% yoy
High-tech drives industrial output as manufacturing moves up value chain
China’s industrial sector continues to show resilience, with high production output driven by strong growth in tech-related sectors. Overall industrial output increased 5.5 percent year-on-year in September, averaging 5.3 percent across the first three quarters of the year. The added value of manufacturing increased by 6 percent year-on-year in September, with high-tech manufacturing reaching 15.3 percent.
Several high-tech products exhibited particularly rapid growth, with production of 3D printing equipment, Li-ion batteries, and industrial robot products growing 62.5 percent, 39.5 percent, and 29.1 percent, respectively.
Manufacturing of machinery also continued to post robust growth in September across several sub-sectors, including general-purpose machinery (up 8.5 percent year-on-year), special-purpose machinery (up 12.1 percent), automobiles (up 6.7 percent), and electrical machinery and equipment (up 8.1 percent).
China’s factory-gate prices continued to grow, exhibiting a month-on-month increase of 1.2 percent in September and accelerating 0.8 percentage points from August. On an annual basis, prices increased 5 percent in September. While this uptick may signal growing industrial demand, it is also likely to be driven in large part by rising costs as a result of global supply chain disruptions and rising demand for key tech products from AI-led growth.
What this means for businesses
China’s accelerating shift toward high-tech, higher-value manufacturing creates opportunities for foreign companies that supply advanced components, production equipment, industrial software, and specialised technologies. Strong growth in batteries, robotics, and 3D printing also points to expanding industrial capacity in sectors that are becoming increasingly important to global supply chains.
At the same time, the rapid expansion of domestic manufacturing capabilities in high-tech sectors is intensifying competition for foreign suppliers, while rising factory-gate prices signal changing input costs and pricing conditions across industrial supply chains.
Consumers trade in demand in goods for services
China’s domestic consumer demand for goods has remained sluggish throughout 2026, with retail sales of goods growing just 1.1 percent in the first nine months of the year and at the same rate in September – a small improvement from the 0.4 percent figure recorded in August.
In addition to the subdued domestic demand dating back to the COVID-19 pandemic and the housing slump, recent consumption figures have been dragged down by falls in purchases of big-ticket items, in particular cars and domestic household appliances, which stem from the ending of several government subsidy programs. When removing vehicle sales, retail sales grew 2.8 percent year-on-year in the first nine months of the year and 3.9 percent in September.
Meanwhile, the low demand for goods is increasingly being offset by growing sales of consumer services, in particular communication and information services (online and digital services), travel consulting and rental services, and cultural, sports, and leisure activities, all of which saw higher rates of growth, according to the NBS. Retail sales of services jumped 5 percent year-on-year in the first three quarters.
What this means for businesses
Wang Shoukun, Dean at the School of Economics at Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics, told Xinhua News that consumers are increasingly “reallocating” spending from goods to services, and from big-ticket items to experiences.
Service providers, in particular those in travel, leisure, culture, and digital businesses, may be able to leverage this shift by capturing demand that is moving away from goods. Online services are growing faster than online goods sales (year-to-date, online services have increased at 5.3 percent annually compared to 3.8 percent for online goods), favouring firms that provide virtual experiences or deliver services digitally. This trajectory also has policy backing, with a services consumption work plan released in February 2026 focusing on sectors such as transport, travel – including inbound tourism – vehicle after-sales, and sports and entertainment.
Meanwhile, makers of goods with exposure to China’s domestic market will face weaker sales, particularly in subsidy-driven categories like cars and household appliances. They are likely to compete harder on price, accept thinner margins, or rely more heavily on imports, as is already the case for car producers.
Tech-led growth drives surge in foreign trade
China’s foreign trade has continued the rapid upward trajectory of recent months, buoyed by the continually expanding demand for high-tech products. Exports in September reached US$447.18 billion, up 36.3 percent year-on-year, according to data from China Customs. Imports also surged, increasing 31 percent year-on-year to US$313.65 billion.
In the first three quarters, total foreign trade reached US$5.8 trillion, up 23.8 percent from the same period in 2025, with exports totaling US$3.37 trillion (up 23.8 percent) and imports US$2.43 trillion (up 27.5 percent).

The uptick in exports in September was driven by high-tech shipments, with this broad category of goods increasing 63.9 percent from the previous year.
Integrated circuit (IC) exports in September skyrocketed in an indication of AI-led demand, increasing 136.3 percent year-on-year by value to US$44.95 billion. By volume, however, exports grew just 1.2 percent to 32.6 billion units. Meanwhile, 3D printer exports increased 123.3 percent by value and 119.6 percent by volume.
Storage batteries also saw a jump in exports, increasing 47.5 percent year-on-year by volume and 56.8 percent by value in September, of which Li-ion batteries grew 53.3 percent in value and 57.9 percent in volume.
What this means for businesses
Overall trade value figures may be somewhat distorted by the rising value of key goods, in particular ICs. The sharp rise in value while volume stayed roughly flat points to the global chip shortage driven by demand from the construction of AI data centres, although more trade in higher-end products may also impact overall trade value. This trade growth is therefore vulnerable to sudden changes in demand. At the same time, if prices keep rising, higher memory costs could feed into competing products such as smartphones and dampen overall consumer demand for key Chinese exports.
Nonetheless, export volumes remain high across several high-tech categories (such as 3D printers and batteries), as well as traditional sectors such as factory machinery, indicating output and demand are robust in other key sectors
For companies, the price increases mean continued margin pressure for device makers that buy memory. Because suppliers are prioritising capacity for AI servers, output of consumer devices is limited, and sustained price rises could in turn weaken demand.

articles.title: Local production, logistics reshape Saudi food supply chains - Arab News
articles.summary: Local production, logistics reshape Saudi food supply chains  Arab News
articles.full_text:
- 43rd edition of Saudi Agriculture Exhibition in Riyadh runs until Oct. 22
RIYADH: From refrigerated trucks carrying fresh produce from Al-Kharj to strategically located warehouses stocked with grain reserves, Saudi Arabia is quietly reshaping the way food moves across the Kingdom.
Industry leaders speaking at the Saudi Agriculture Exhibition 2026 said food security was no longer focused solely on securing supplies from abroad. Increasingly, the emphasis is on growing more food locally, strengthening logistics networks and building supply chains capable of withstanding disruptions.
The Minister of Environment, Water and Agriculture Abdulrahman Al-Fadli inaugurated the 43rd edition of the Saudi Agriculture Exhibition in Riyadh on Monday. Held under the theme “An Integrated Agricultural Ecosystem for a Sustainable Future,” the exhibition runs until Oct. 22 and brings together local and international companies from across the sector.
During the opening ceremony, Al-Fadli witnessed the signing of several agreements and memorandums of understanding between government and semi-government entities, private-sector organizations and international companies aimed at supporting agriculture and food production, accelerating the adoption of new technologies and contributing to economic growth.
For Wang Dan, general manager of First Impression Agricultural Company, the future lies in combining local production with reliable cold-chain networks.
She said: “Saudi Arabia's food supply chains are becoming increasingly focused on local production and resilience.”
She said the company’s strategy centered on producing locally while maintaining close coordination with suppliers and customers to respond quickly to shifts in demand and market conditions.
“The company’s approach is to strengthen local production, plan supplies carefully, and maintain close coordination with suppliers and customers, which helps respond to changing conditions and support continuity of supply,” she added.
Wang said refrigerated storage facilities and delivery vehicles played a crucial role in preserving freshness, linking production sites in Al-Kharj with customers across the Kingdom.
“Logistics are being developed around coordinated production, cold storage, and refrigerated delivery, with a focus on improving delivery planning, reducing delays, and minimizing product losses,” she said.
By reducing waste and ensuring a steady flow of locally grown produce, such systems can help keep fresh food available even during periods of disruption, she added.
The same focus on resilience is shaping larger regional food networks.
Ahmed Al-Suwaidi, chief corporate affairs officer at Al Dahra Group, said Saudi Arabia had invested heavily in logistics infrastructure, storage, agricultural technology and food processing as it pursued its Vision 2030 and food security goals.
“The Kingdom is strengthening its position as a leading regional player in building modern agricultural value chains connecting sourcing, storage, logistics, processing, and distribution,” he said.
According to Al-Suwaidi, resilience depends on more than production alone. Diversified sourcing, multiple logistics routes, strategic inventory management and coordination across operations have become essential safeguards against supply disruptions.
He said Al Dahra’s warehousing and storage facilities in Riyadh, Qassim and Jeddah helped position inventory closer to customers nationwide, supported by predictive planning, multimodal transport networks and diversified trade routes.
Strategic reserves remain a key part of the equation. Al-Suwaidi pointed to Al Dahra’s Fujairah Strategic Grain Terminal, which has a storage capacity of around 300,000 tonnes.
He said: “Integrating sourcing, storage, processing, and distribution helps ensure strategic reserves remain accessible, strengthening food system resilience across the GCC and supporting national food security strategies, including Saudi Arabia’s long-term ambitions.”
As Saudi Arabia pushes to build a more self-reliant agricultural sector, industry leaders say the future of food security will depend not only on what is produced, but on how efficiently it can be stored, transported and delivered to consumers across the Kingdom.

articles.title: Navigating New Global Trade Dynamics: Supply Chains and Emerging Trade Corridors - FTI Consulting
articles.summary: Navigating New Global Trade Dynamics: Supply Chains and Emerging Trade Corridors  FTI Consulting
articles.full_text:
- October 21, 2026
Amid intensifying competition and tension between major economic powers, middle economies are increasingly pursuing alternate economic and trade relationships, driven by a need for both greater strategic autonomy and deeper cooperation with one another. With a weakened United Nations (“UN”), World Trade Organization (“WTO”) and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (“NATO”) architecture and continuing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and Ukraine, the year ahead will likely see further instability affecting key trade, energy and agricultural corridors, leading to continued shifting political winds and increased protectionist tendencies.
Through a range of regional, bilateral and multilateral platforms, economies outside of the ‘G2’ United States-China axis are establishing landmark Global North-Global South trade relationships. The 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Canada’s proposed European Union associate membership and Free Trade Agreements (“FTA”) signed by the EU and India are recent examples recent efforts to strengthen economic resilience in the face of these global developments by diversifying partnerships and giving emerging and middle economies greater agency within global governance.
For businesses operating across sectors such as technology, advanced manufacturing, clean energy, mobility and consumer goods, these developments may create new pathways for growth while reshaping existing trade and investment relationships. As economic cooperation expands across emerging and middle power economies, companies will need to evaluate new market opportunities, regulatory requirements and the potential to diversify supply chains and partnerships across markets.
The BRICS Summit Under India’s Chairmanship
Despite its share of sceptics, BRICS, an economic and political alliance alternative to NATO and G7, has given the Global South a greater voice in its lobal economic and governance discussions. Iran and the UAE backed the BRICS statement urging restraint in the Middle East during the 2026 Summit global economic and governance discussions,1 highlighting the bloc’s diplomatic significance. Meanwhile, China, India and Russia continue to pursue their respective interests and influence within the bloc During the summit.2 While the actual implementation of this cooperation is forthcoming, these goals are harbingers of how trade negotiations between the Global North and Global South could play out in the long term.
At the end of the summit, the Global South agenda highlighted:
Industrial Growth
- Frame BRICS Guiding Principles for Credit Assessment Frameworks for Export-oriented micro, small and medium enterprises (“MSMEs”), and build an Invoice Discounting Mechanism for BRICS members to facilitate invoice discounting and strengthen MSME participation in international trade.3
- Establish UN Industrial Development Organization (“UNIDO”)-supported BRICS Centre for Industrial Competencies, supported by national centres, including China and India.4
- Explore a proposed BRICS New Investment Platform to facilitate greater investment cooperation across member economies.5
- Advance BRICS collaboration on low-carbon hydrogen and a joint report on hydrogen value chains.6
Technology
- Expand cross-border payments through BRICS Payment Task Force, including greater interoperability of payment systems and messaging channels, and use of local currencies in trade and investment.7
- Progress plans for BRICS submarine cable infrastructure and a technical and economic feasibility study to establish a high-speed communication network.8
- Strengthen cyber resilience in the financial sector through a BRICS Rapid Information Security Channel and annual cyber exercises.9
Agriculture
- Launch the BRICS Agro-Inputs, Genetic Resources and Information Network (“AGRIN”) and a Global Forum on Farmers’ Rights in Seed Systems.10
- Establish BRICS Network of Centres of Excellence on Agroecology and Regenerative Agriculture for Climate Resilience and Productivity, and a BRICS Network on Digital Agriculture.11
- Establish BRICS Grain Exchange, with potential expansion into other products.12
Trade and Global Governance
- Support reform of the UN (including the UN Security Council) and the WTO13
- Oppose indiscriminate tariffs, non-tariff barriers and protectionist measures, including those justified on environmental grounds inconsistent with WTO rules14
Implications For Trade, Tech and Industrial Supply Chains
Broader trade and economic arrangements, such as the India-EU FTA, EU-MERCOSUR FTA and Canada-EU Associate Membership discussions, illustrate a wider trend towards economic diversification and the strengthening of regional and cross-regional partnerships. Alongside initiatives focused on resilient supply chains, local-currency settlement, digital public infrastructure, AI and low-carbon value chains, these developments signal the gradual emergence of alternative economic systems. Taken together, they point to a more diversified global economic architecture, with implications for sourcing, market access, technology partnerships, financing channels and regulatory requirements for businesses. This trend is also reflected in the financing mechanisms supporting these markets. At the BRICS Summit, the New Development Bank (“NDB”) announced plans to scale up local-currency financing, diversify its capital sources and mobilise resources for regional infrastructure projects.15 As these economic ties deepen and intra-bloc market access expands, global and domestic businesses can position themselves for growth by considering three key areas and their implications.
Cross-Border Trade Between India, China and Brazil
Rising intra-member investment between BRICS members, supported by initiatives such as the BRICS Centre for Industrial Competencies and the proposed New Investment Platform, is reshaping supplier ecosystems, joint-venture structures and manufacturing capacity across strategic sectors. While Chinese investment remains an important component of this trend, companies should view emerging BRICS-linked investment flows as part of a wider push to strengthen South-South industrial cooperation and market access. The key implication is the emergence of alternative South-South supply chains that could challenge traditional trade lanes, while creating new partnership and market-access opportunities for companies able to navigate local security, regulatory and industrial-policy priorities.
- India-China Trade: Heightened national security screening requires clear joint-venture (“JV”) structuring and local partnership alignment. India continues to apply enhanced scrutiny to investments requiring government approval, with approximately USD1.18 billion approved under the government approval route in FY25 to FY2616 Strategic JV structures in electronics manufacturing may offer a template for participation in sectors subject to heightened regulatory and security review.
- China-Brazil Trade: Chinese investment in Brazil reached USD6.1 billion across 52 projects in 2025, with heavy concentration in power, mining and e‑mobility.17 Mining outlays more than tripled to USD1.76 billion, while 31 green/sustainability projects (hydropower, solar, wind, electric vehicles) set a new record.18 This deepens China’s role in critical minerals and electric mobility in Brazil and, across Latin America, intensifies competitive pressure on Western original equipment manufacturers in green tech.
- Brazil-India Trade: The opening of high-value South-South supply chains beyond traditional Western trade lanes, together with greater investment in aerospace, defence, IT services and critical minerals, demonstrates these relationships are expanding beyond commodities into strategic and digital technologies.
Brazil offers a particularly resilient, commodity‑anchored platform for supply‑chain diversification into 2027 to 2029, with increasing access to China and EU markets under the interim EU-Mercosur trade agreement (in force since May 2026) and the new Mercosur-EFTA deal (effective October 2026).
19, 20 As a self‑assertive middle power, Brazil is pursuing a multi‑alignment strategy (balancing the United States and China while amplifying its role in BRICS, the G20 and South‑South cooperation) to preserve strategic autonomy and diversify trade and technology partners.
However, the October 2026 presidential election adds near‑term policy and fiscal uncertainty, with debt above approximately 75% of GDP, contested adjustment paths and ongoing implementation of the VAT‑style tax reform.
21 The next administration’s choices on foreign policy, fiscal consolidation, industrial policy and trade regulation will establish the risk premium and investment climate for 2027 to 2030, even as Brazil currently deepens South‑South linkages (e.
g.
, Africa, BRICS) and seeks to move up global value chains beyond commodities.
Opportunities exist in agribusiness, mining, aerospace and advanced manufacturing.
However, companies should consider a phased approach to investment and growth, supported by scenario planning around post‑election fiscal signals, microeconomic reforms and Brazil’s evolving foreign economic strategy.
For supply‑chain leaders, Brazil is a strategic, though more complex, option to reduce concentration risk while monitoring regulatory, macro and geopolitical developments through the 2027 to 2029 planning cycle.

While BRICS cooperation is expanding across trade, industrial development and investment facilitation, companies should distinguish between the bloc’s strategic agenda and the regulatory realities of individual markets. Investment screening mechanisms, localisation requirements, technology-transfer expectations, data governance rules and sector-specific industrial policies will remain important considerations for sourcing, manufacturing and investment decisions across member economies.
